All three RCTs were multicentric studies. Vink 2019 was conducted in Canada, the Czech Republic, France, the Republic of Korea, and the UK, while the other two RCTs did not report any details about the study sites ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ). The studies included 3054 participants with solid tumours recruited between November 2007 to April 2017. The mean age ranged between 55.8 to 64 years (range 35 to 83), and 64.6% of the participants were female. In two RCTs, participants were randomised to receive four doses of inactivated ( Mullane 2019 ) or heat‐treated ( Mullane 2013 ) varicella zoster vaccine, 30 days apart, compared to placebo. In Vink 2019 , participants were randomised to receive either two doses of an adjuvant recombinant zoster vaccine 30 to 60 days apart or placebo. One study reported data on the incidence of herpes zoster (mean 2.45 years after final dose) defined as confirmed herpes zoster (confirmed by skin lesion PCR, if available, or by adjudication of the clinical case description by the clinical adjudication committee) and all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after final dose ( Mullane 2019 ). All three RCTs reported data on safety outcomes, such as any adverse events and serious adverse events up to 30 days after final dose ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ). Additional outcomes included antibody response ( Mullane 2013 ; Vink 2019 ), cell‐mediated immune response ( Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ), and moderate‐to‐severe herpes zoster‐associated pain, herpes zoster complications, postherpetic neuralgia, and the number of participants with study medication withdrawn due to an adverse event ( Mullane 2019 ). The three RCTs were funded by the manufacturers of the vaccines ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ). Studies of vaccines for the prevention of influenza Goldmann 2015 was a double‐blind RCT conducted in one centre in Germany. Four studies were prospective controlled NRSIs ( Amdisen 2024 ; Gögenur 2021 ; INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ). Three studies were open‐label and conducted in multiple centres in Italy ( INVIDIa‐2 ), Denmark ( Gögenur 2021 ), and the Netherlands ( Wijn 2018 ). Amdisen 2024 was a nationwide register‐based study conducted in Denmark. Altogether, the studies included data from 76,372 participants with solid tumours receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (alone or in combination) ( INVIDIa‐2 ), participants with lung cancer receiving nivolumab ( Wijn 2018 ), participants with solid tumours scheduled for surgery ( Gögenur 2021 ), participants who were scheduled for surgery of neck or oesophageal cancer ( Goldmann 2015 ), and participants with an incident cancer diagnosis from 1 October 2002 to 1 October 2017 in the Danish Cancer Registry ( Amdisen 2024 ). In Amdisen 2024 , all participants received chemotherapy. Participants were recruited between November 2005 to January 2020 ( Gögenur 2021 ; INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ). In Amdisen 2024 , the study period spanned from the introduction of the free‐of‐charge influenza vaccine for individuals with acquired immunodeficiency in the 2007/2008 season until the 2017/2018 season. The mean age ranged between 56.5 (SD 8.8) to 64.4 years (SD 7.8), and 6.1% to 55.3% of the participants were female ( INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ). In Goldmann 2015 , participants were randomised to receive either two doses of an influenza vaccine (Mutagrip; Sanofi Pasteur) or placebo, administered on the day before surgery and the day of surgery. In the controlled NRSIs, participants received single doses of a trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine (influenza season 2015/2016 and 2016/2017) ( Wijn 2018 ), trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine ( Gögenur 2021 ), or trivalent adjuvant, trivalent non‐adjuvant, or quadrivalent non‐adjuvant influenza vaccine (influenza season 2019/2020) ( INVIDIa‐2 ) compared to no vaccine. In Gögenur 2021 , 26.2% of participants received the vaccine within 30 days post‐surgery, while 73.8% were vaccinated within 180 days of surgery. Amdisen 2024 gathered data on influenza vaccination dates from three Danish registries: the Danish National Health Service Register for free vaccinations administered by general practitioners, the Danish National Patient Registry for vaccinations during hospitalisation, and the Danish National Prescription Registry for vaccines redeemed at pharmacies. Notably, one individual could have been included in more than one influenza season. Two studies reported the incidence of influenza ( Amdisen 2024 ; INVIDIa‐2 ). In Amdisen 2024 , the outcome was defined as influenza requiring treatment based on an influenza diagnosis recorded in the Danish National Patient Registry or a prescription for oseltamivir documented in the Danish National Prescription Registry. In INVIDIa‐2 , the outcome was defined as a severe illness, characterised by sudden and rapid onset of one or more general symptoms, such as fever or low‐grade fever, malaise, and/or fatigue, headaches, myalgia, and at least one respiratory symptom such as cough, sore throat, or dyspnoea. Two studies reported all‐cause mortality 15 days post‐surgery and from 180 days to three years post‐surgery ( Gögenur 2021 ; Goldmann 2015 ), while Amdisen 2024 reported all‐cause mortality for up to five years after the first cancer diagnosis or until the end of the study period (31 March 2018), whichever came first. Two studies reported adverse events ( Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ). Additional outcomes include duration of hospital and ICU stay, mHLA‐DR expression of monocytes, postoperative incidence of infections ( Goldmann 2015 ); time to influenza‐like illness, Influenza‐free survival, vaccine cover rate, incidence of bacterial complications, infection recrudescence, clinically diagnosed complications/ superinfections during the influenza episode, hospital admissions, and need for intravenous therapy for influenza‐like illness, duration of influenza symptoms, influenza‐like illness fatality rate, usage rate for the quick test/nasal/pharyngeal swab or viral serology in people with influenza‐like illness, disease control rate, objective response rate, time to treatment failure, progression‐free survival, overall survival, immune‐related toxicity ( INVIDIa‐2 ); immune‐related adverse events and serious adverse events, discontinuation owing to immune‐related serious adverse events, progression, or clinical deterioration ( Wijn 2018 ); pneumonia, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, venous thromboembolism ( Amdisen 2024 ). INVIDIa‐2 was funded by the manufacturer of the vaccine, whereas Goldmann 2015 received funding from inner university grants. Amdisen 2024 received public funding from the Danish Cancer Research Foundation and the Danish Cancer Society. Two studies did not disclose their funding sources ( Gögenur 2021 ; Wijn 2018 ). Studies of vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 Thomas 2022 was a triple‐blind RCT conducted in multiple centres across the USA, Argentina, Brazil, Germany, South Africa, and Turkey. Zhao 2024 was a prospective controlled multicentric NRSI conducted in China. Altogether, the studies included data from 2397 participants with solid tumours. In Thomas 2022 , the total population originally was 46,429 healthy participants aged over 12 years. However, participants with pre‐existing stable neoplasia, including solid tumours and haematological malignancies, were also eligible to participate in the study. For this population, Thomas 2022 analysed the data in a post‐hoc subgroup analysis. Zhao 2024 included participants with hepatocellular carcinoma. Participants were recruited between July 2020 and January 2021 ( Thomas 2022 ) or between January 2022 and October 2022 ( Zhao 2024 ). Based on the recruitment periods, we assume that participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta, and gamma ( Thomas 2022 ) or omicron ( Zhao 2024 ). The mean age ranged between 59.2 (SD 11) and 62 years (SD 11.8). In Thomas 2022 , most participants (62.7% to 63.9%) were female, whereas in Zhao 2024 , only 17.6% to 20.6% were female. In Thomas 2022 , participants were randomised to receive either two doses of BNT162b2 or placebo. In Zhao 2024 , participants received at least one dose of various vaccines, including CoronaVac, BBIBP‐CorV, Ad5‐nCoV, BNT162b2, ZF2001 (an adjuvant protein subunit vaccine, not authorised by the EMA or authorised in at least 10 countries worldwide) or no vaccine. Each of these vaccines typically consists of two doses. Notably, 44.9% of the participants completed the full two‐dose regimen, while 48.6% received a booster vaccination. Some of the participants (6.5%) had only one dose and were therefore not fully vaccinated. Thomas 2022 reported the incidence of COVID‐19, defined as a positive reverse transcription chain reaction (RT‐PCR) or nucleic acid amplification technology (NAAT) test in participants without previous SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, and in participants with and without previous SARS‐CoV‐2 infection from seven days up to six months after the second dose. Additionally, the study reported adverse events and serious adverse events in a mixed population of individuals with solid tumours and haematological malignancies who had a past or ongoing malignancy. Zhao 2024 reported on the incidence of COVID‐19, defined as the rate of SARS‐CoV‐2 infections over a median follow‐up period of 16.3 months (interquartile range (IQR) 14.2 to 19.3). However, it was not specified whether SARS‐CoV‐2 infections were confirmed by testing. The study also provided data on all‐cause mortality. Additional outcomes included vaccine efficacy ( Thomas 2022 ), overall survival, infection‐free survival, severe or very severe SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, and vaccine‐related adverse events ( Zhao 2024 ). Thomas 2022 received funding from the manufacturer of the vaccine, while Zhao 2024 was supported by public funding. Ongoing studies We identified two ongoing studies, which the study registrations classified as ‘recruiting’ ( NCT05774171 ) or 'recruitment completed' ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) (see Characteristics of ongoing studies ). NCT05774171 is a prospective cohort study evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines compared to no vaccine in participants with past or current tumours, regardless of tumour type. The target sample size is 700 participants, and the planned completion date is recorded as December 2023. ACTRN12622000706774 is an open‐label RCT investigating an influenza vaccine compared to no vaccine in participants undergoing major abdominal cancer surgery. The target sample size is 54 participants and the planned completion date is recorded as March 2024. Discussion Summary of main results This review aimed to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours. Altogether, we identified 10 studies for inclusion in this review. Most studies included adults with malignant solid tumours of different types. Of these, three RCTs (3054 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster, five studies (one RCT and four controlled NRSIs; 76,372 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza, and one RCT (2256 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent COVID‐19. The RCTs assessing herpes zoster and COVID‐19 vaccines were funded by the manufacturers of the vaccines. We assessed the RCTs as being at low or moderate risk of bias, while we judged most of the controlled NRSIs to be at critical risk of bias, primarily due to concerns about confounding. Further, we identified two ongoing studies: one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine and one controlled NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines. We also identified one completed but not yet published study, and 11 studies await classification due to unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest, results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination. We did not identify RCTs or controlled NRSIs on vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. In the following, only the results from RCTs are presented. Results from controlled NRSIs are detailed in the Effects of interventions section of the main text. Effects of interventions Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 1 . Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster decrease the incidence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster probably make little or no difference in all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after the final dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster make little or no difference in adverse events (any grade) up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence) and probably make little or no difference in serious adverse events up to 30 days (moderate certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster increase the number of participants with localised events at the injection site up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster may have little or no difference in the number of participants with systemic events up to 30 days after the final dose (low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 2 . We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on all‐cause mortality up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza in adverse events (any grade) up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on serious adverse events up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 3 . Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in participants without previous COVID‐19 infection up to six months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably increase the number of participants with adverse events (any grade) up to 6 months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 may make little or no difference in the number of participants with serious adverse events up to 6 months after the second dose (low‐certainty evidence). Overall completeness and applicability of evidence The evidence summarised in this systematic review applies to vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster, influenza, and COVID‐19 in adults with solid tumours. The findings are particularly relevant for healthcare providers involved in the care of these people, as they can guide vaccination strategies aimed at reducing infection risk. Understanding vaccine efficacy and safety is crucial for adults with solid tumours when making informed health decisions. The review indicates that certain vaccines, specifically those for herpes zoster and COVID‐19, demonstrate high‐ or moderate‐certainty evidence for reducing infection incidence. However, these vaccines may be associated with localised events at the injection site or any‐grade adverse events. It is important to note that the applicability of these findings may vary based on specific types of malignancy and their stages. Additionally, cancer therapies can significantly impact immune function and vaccine efficacy. However, due to insufficient data, we could not determine whether there are differences in outcomes between various malignancies or cancer therapies. The RCTs on herpes zoster included adults with diverse solid tumour types, such as breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and lung cancer ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ), all receiving chemotherapy. This diversity allows for some comparison regarding how chemotherapy impacts vaccine efficacy across different cancers. Additionally, there are variations in vaccine types used in these studies. In Mullane 2013 , participants received a heat‐treated zoster vaccine, while Mullane 2019 administered an inactivated varicella‐zoster virus vaccine. In contrast, Vink 2019 employed an adjuvant recombinant zoster vaccine. A distinction in vaccine types may be important because different formulations can elicit varying immune responses, which may impact their effectiveness. In contrast to the herpes zoster vaccines, the RCT on influenza vaccines focused on adults with neck and oesophageal cancers undergoing surgery ( Goldmann 2015 ). This may limit the generalisability of the findings to other cancer types or treatment modalities, since participants were vaccinated prior to surgery. While there is very low certainty in the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of influenza vaccination for this particular subset of patients, it may not directly apply to those receiving immunotherapy or other surgical interventions. To supplement our findings from Goldmann 2015 , which was published as correspondence, we incorporated data from controlled NRSIs. For instance, INVIDIa‐2 and Amdisen 2024 reported on the incidence of influenza across a wider range of cancers, including participants undergoing immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy or chemotherapy. However, the studies primarily focused on severe disease and may not capture milder cases or asymptomatic infections, which are also important for assessing vaccine efficacy. In contrast, the data from controlled NRSI suggests that there is an effect on all‐cause mortality (moderate‐certainty) ( Gögenur 2021 ). This difference may arise from the different populations and the timing of the vaccination analysed in the included studies. Gögenur 2021 focuses on post‐surgery vaccination across multiple cancer types scheduled for surgery. The timing of the vaccination was within 30 days post‐surgery. The study measured all‐cause mortality as an outcome 180 days to three years post‐surgery. Nevertheless, this long‐term follow‐up provides insights into the potential impact of post‐surgery influenza vaccination on survival outcomes, thereby enhancing the completeness of results. However, while this study increases applicability by addressing diverse patient populations, it is essential to consider that factors influencing mortality may be multifactorial and not solely attributable to vaccination status. With respect to any‐grade adverse events, there remains uncertainty regarding the effects of influenza vaccines as indicated by both RCT ( Goldmann 2015 ) and controlled NRSI ( Wijn 2018 ) data. Wijn 2018 focused on adults with lung cancer receiving nivolumab. The study provides insights into the interactions between seasonal influenza vaccination and immunotherapy, but their targeted nature may restrict generalisability to other cancer treatments or patient populations not undergoing similar therapies. Influenza viruses are constantly evolving, and new strains can emerge. Influenza vaccines are adjusted annually to ensure better efficacy against the currently circulating strains ( WHO 2024 ). Therefore, it is important to interpret our findings on influenza vaccines with caution, as the included studies cover various influenza seasons. For example, the study by INVIDIa‐2 focuses on the 2019/2020 influenza season, while Wijn 2018 investigates the 2015/2016 and 2016/2017 seasons and Amdisen 2024 covers the seasons 2007/2008 to 2017/2018. Gögenur 2021 recruited participants between 2010 and 2015, and Goldmann 2015 covers the period from 2005 to 2008. This variability means that studies conducted across different seasons may yield results that are not directly comparable or applicable to current strains circulating within specific populations. In terms of COVID‐19 vaccines, Thomas 2022 focused on adults with various solid tumours, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, but did not provide clear information about specific cancer treatments received by the participants. We used data from a mixed population of solid tumours and haematological malignancies for adverse events and serious adverse events analyses since we expect similar events across both groups ( Copeland 2024 ; Javadinia 2022 ). Based on the RCT data, COVID‐19 vaccines probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 (moderate‐certainty). As the data only originates from a post‐hoc subgroup analysis, we supplemented our findings with data from controlled NRSIs. In contrast, controlled NRSI data presents uncertainty regarding their effects. The controlled NRSI by Zhao 2024 , specifically examined adults with hepatocellular carcinoma, a group facing unique immunological challenges due to liver dysfunction and underlying viral infections (e.g. hepatitis), which could influence vaccine efficacy differently than in other solid tumours ( Sachdeva 2015 ). Moreover, differences in vaccination regimens complicate comparisons. Thomas 2022 used the BNT162b2 vaccine, while Zhao 2024 , included multiple vaccines such as CoronaVac, BBIBP‐CorV, Zifivax, Convidecia, and BNT162b2. Notably, in Zhao 2024 , a small proportion of participants (6.5%) were not fully vaccinated. Such an incomplete vaccination status could lead to underestimating the potential protective effect of vaccination against infection. Furthermore, Thomas 2022 recruited participants between July 2020 to January 2021. Based on the recruitment period, we assume that participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta and gamma. In contrast, Zhao 2024 recruited participants between January 2022 and October 2022 where omicron was prevalent. The evidence is only applicable to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants prevalent at the time of the studies. It is also crucial for consumers and caregivers to be aware of the limitations regarding other vaccines due to insufficient data. Although there is a lack of evidence or only low to very low‐certainty evidence for many of the vaccines we were interested in for this particular group of adults with solid tumours, studies involving immunocompetent adults generally demonstrate that vaccines are well tolerated and effective in preventing severe outcomes and providing protection ( Demicheli 2018 ; Graña 2022 ; Plosker 2015 ). Due to the small number of included studies and lack of subgroup data in the primary studies, we were unable to adequately investigate the influence of effect modifiers, such as type of malignancy or treatment, through subgroup analyses. While most studies measure immunogenicity parameters such as antibody levels, seroconversion, or T‐cell responses, there are no correlates of protection defined. These surrogate endpoints are not considered as patient‐relevant outcomes. In this review, we focused only on patient‐relevant outcomes that we determined in a workshop conducted with people with cancer and their representatives. The involvement of adults with cancer and their representatives was essential to obtain a better understanding of patient‐important outcomes, to ensure a patient‐relevant focus for this systematic review, and to ensure that our findings remain relevant to consumers navigating complex healthcare decisions. Notably, none of the included studies measured quality of life. The studies included in our review were predominantly conducted in high‐income countries, which may not fully represent the challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). According to Kamboj 2024 , the availability, accessibility, and utilisation of vaccines amongst adults with cancer in LMICs present significant hurdles. Limited resources and infrastructure, along with logistical barriers, often hinder vaccine distribution in these regions. Additionally, the high cost of vaccines can render them financially unattainable for many individuals. Consequently, the lack of access to vaccines leaves individuals with cancer in LMICs vulnerable to serious infections, which can adversely impact their health outcomes. Our review identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one controlled NRSI ( NCT05774171 ) evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines, which may provide further insights into vaccine efficacy once they are completed. One RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine has been completed, but no results have been published yet ( NCT02998736 ). We further categorised 12 studies with unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest or results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination as 'awaiting classification' ( Bettinger 2022 ; EPIVAC ; Hayashi 2023 ; Kazemain 2023 ; Khaddour 2022 ; Klastersky 1986 ; Lau 2022 ; Leuva 2022 ; NCT01698177 ; NL‐OMON32477 ; Serrano 2022 ; Vinograd 2013 ). EPIVAC , a comprehensive population‐based cohort study, assessed the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines and provided data categorised for individuals with compromised immune systems. These encompass solid tumours, haematological malignancies, chronic severe nephropathy, asplenia, immunodeficiency (including HIV), and long‐term corticosteroid therapy or other immunosuppressive drugs. Since the data for these conditions were not analysed separately, we were unable to include the study. We will consider including these studies in an update of this review once results or sufficient information is available. Furthermore, we excluded numerous controlled NRSIs in which healthy individuals were used as a control group (e.g. Gomez 2021 ; Silveira 2019 ). Quality of the evidence Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from three RCTs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as high to low (see Table 1 ). We have high certainty in the evidence for the outcomes of incidence of herpes zoster, adverse events of any grade, and localised events at the injection site, and moderate certainty for the outcomes of all‐cause mortality and serious adverse events. Our main concern was imprecision due to wide confidence intervals. We have low certainty in the identified evidence for systemic events. We downgraded the certainty of the evidence for imprecision due to a wide confidence interval and inconsistency due to substantial statistical heterogeneity. Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT and four controlled NRSIs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low (see Table 2 ). For the RCT, we rated the certainty of the evidence as very low. Our main concerns were the risk of bias due to missing information on allocation concealment, missing data, selection of the reported results, and imprecision due to very wide confidence intervals, low number of participants, and low number of events (all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, and serious adverse events). For controlled NRSIs, we rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low. We downgraded the evidence for risk of bias due to confounding (incidence of influenza, all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade) and imprecision due to wide confidence intervals (incidence of influenza, adverse events of any grade). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to low (see Table 3 ). Our main concerns were imprecision due to a low number of events or wide confidence intervals (incidence of COVID‐19, serious adverse events), or indirectness due to a mixed population including participants with solid tumours and haematological malignancies (any‐grade adverse events and serious adverse events). Potential biases in the review process We followed the guidelines of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions to minimise several potential biases in the review process ( Higgins 2024a ). An experienced information specialist (IM) developed the peer‐reviewed search strategy. The sensitive search included relevant electronic databases, as well as clinical trial registries, to ensure comprehensive coverage of available literature. To uphold the integrity and reliability of our review process, we conducted a comprehensive search for errata and retractions related to the studies included in our analysis. This step was essential for identifying potential biases arising from flawed or retracted research that could impact our conclusions. To supplement the lack of RCTs, we performed searches for controlled NRSIs when no RCTs were available for vaccines targeting specific infectious diseases. This also included vaccines to prevent influenza and COVID‐19, as the identified RCTs were published as correspondence ( Goldmann 2015 ) or reported data on solid tumour participants in a post hoc subgroup analysis ( Thomas 2022 ). While correspondence and post hoc analyses might provide valuable insights, they are generally considered less informative compared to primary research articles. Due to the limitations of these publication types, we decided to search for controlled NRSI as well. Given the differences in study design and potential biases associated with controlled NRSIs, we did not pool data from RCTs and controlled NRSIs. In addition, we made a conscious decision to categorise eligible studies that did not report any relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification' rather than including or excluding them without having explored other ways to establish if our outcomes had been measured. This change reflects our commitment to ensuring that only studies with pertinent outcome data contribute to our findings. We included only studies with a minimum sample size of 20 participants per arm. This criterion was established to enhance the reliability and generalisability of our findings by ensuring that included studies had sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful effects. However, this inclusion criterion may also limit the number of available studies, potentially introducing bias if smaller but relevant studies are excluded from consideration (e.g. Chu 2013 ; Kumar 2012 ). In classifying interventions and outcomes, we based our decisions on the data available from the studies. We categorised the studies according to their design (RCTs versus controlled NRSIs) and focused on outcomes that were deemed important by adults with cancer and their representatives. Further, we distinguished between 'localised events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' as separate outcomes. Nonetheless, it is important to note that some studies reported symptoms such as headache or fever as single outcomes, which limited our ability to analyse these effects together ( Thomas 2022 ; Zhao 2024 ). In our analysis, we aimed to capture long‐term outcomes by using the longest available follow‐up data. However, this approach may present limitations, particularly due to variability in follow‐up durations across studies. Such differences may lead to inconsistencies in outcome reporting, introduce potential biases in assessing long‐term effects, and challenges in comparing results between studies with varying timeframes. In cases of missing data, if we needed more information, we contacted the study authors for additional data or relevant details. We received answers from the contact authors of three studies ( Amdisen 2024 ; Leuva 2022 ; Mullane 2013 ). However, we could not use the data from Leuva 2022 due to unclear follow‐up time after a full vaccination. The data from Amdisen 2024 were measured as incidence rates per 10,000 person‐years for the outcomes of incidence of influenza and all‐cause mortality. Due to the incompatible format of these outcomes, we only provide a narrative description, without assessing the risk of bias or certainty of the evidence. Given the small number of studies included in each comparison, the informative value of statistical methods for analysing publication bias, such as funnel plots, was limited. Moreover, due to the small number of included studies, we were unable to conduct any subgroup analyses that might have provided further insights into specific populations or intervention effects. Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews Notably, the ASCO guidelines addressed a research question similar to ours by systematically reviewing studies published between 2013 and 2023 ( Kamboj 2024 ). They focused on adults with solid tumours or haematological malignancies, including long‐term survivors and those who received haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, evaluating routine vaccines listed on the CDC immunisation schedules as well as travel vaccines. Their comparisons included placebo, different vaccines, or varying vaccination strategies. The outcomes assessed encompassed risk of infection, disease severity, mortality, immune responses, and vaccine safety ( Kamboj 2024 ). In terms of herpes zoster vaccines, Kamboj 2024 identified a study concerning solid tumours reporting adverse events ( Vink 2019 ), but did not include Mullane 2013 and Mullane 2019 as the guidelines focused on recombinant zoster vaccines (RZV). RZV, commonly known by its brand name Shingrix, is a recombinant form of glycoprotein E from the varicella‐zoster virus, which is a key protein involved in the virus's ability to infect cells ( Vink 2019 ). Our findings on herpes zoster vaccines align with those of a network meta‐analysis conducted by Xia 2022 , which reported that RZV demonstrated superior efficacy compared to placebo in immunocompromised individuals, achieving 60% efficacy (95% CI 49% to 69%). Adverse events associated with RZV were primarily related to injection site reactions and systemic effects, with no increased risk of serious adverse events or death. Kamboj 2024 indicated that "grade three solicited general adverse events" (i.e. moderate‐to‐severe adverse events actively monitored during the study), were reported by adults with cancer in both the vaccine and placebo arms but were more prevalent in the vaccine arms. This finding is consistent with our observations regarding the safety profile of herpes zoster vaccines. However, it is important to highlight that the analyses by Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 exclusively included studies assessing RZV, while our review encompassed studies assessing heat‐treated zoster vaccines ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ). Additionally, Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 included studies across various immunocompromised conditions such as haematological malignancies, renal transplantation, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and HIV, alongside one study involving individuals with solid tumours ( Vink 2019 ), which was also part of our review. A previous Cochrane review on influenza vaccination conducted by Bitterman 2018 demonstrated that influenza vaccination is associated with reduced mortality and lower rates of infection‐related outcomes compared to non‐vaccination. This review encompassed a diverse population, including adults with solid tumours, haematological malignancies, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The inclusion of such a broad range of immunocompromised groups suggests that influenza vaccination may confer significant benefits across these populations. However, more recent systematic reviews have provided additional insights into the effects of influenza vaccination specifically in adults with cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. For instance, a systematic review by Tsiakos 2022 indicated that influenza vaccination appeared to have no effect on the mortality of adults with cancer receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Furthermore, it presented an acceptable safety profile, as it was not associated with an increased incidence of immune‐related adverse events, whether any grade or serious. In line with this, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 reported that vaccinated adults with cancer exhibited slightly lower rates of immune‐related adverse events compared to unvaccinated adults with cancer (32% versus 41%), reinforcing the notion that vaccination does not exacerbate safety concerns. Despite these findings, both reviews highlight the limitations in available data regarding other efficacy and safety outcomes. Tsiakos 2022 noted that limited data exist concerning progression‐free survival, humoral immunity response, cell‐mediated immunity response, and the incidence of influenza. Similarly, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 provided specific metrics indicating seroprotection rates for different influenza types (78% to 79% for type A and 75% for type B) but did not address these additional outcomes. However, most of the data are derived from observational retrospective studies with small sample sizes and unadjusted analyses ( Lopez‐Olivo 2022 ; Tsiakos 2022 ). The Cochrane review by Graña 2022 concluded that most COVID‐19 vaccines reduce or likely reduce the occurrence of confirmed symptomatic COVID‐19 when compared to placebo. For some vaccines, there is high‐certainty evidence supporting their effectiveness in reducing severe or critical disease. Our findings align with this conclusion, as we also observed a reduction in the incidence of COVID‐19 amongst vaccinated participants without previous infection (moderate‐certainty evidence). Kamboj 2024 further reported numerous studies examining immunologic parameters related to COVID‐19 vaccination amongst adults with cancer. They identified five controlled NRSIs demonstrating reduced rates of hospitalisation and mortality or decreased COVID‐19 sequelae in vaccinated versus unvaccinated adults with cancer. However, these studies did not exclusively focus on adults with solid tumours but also included adults with haematological malignancies ( Kamboj 2024 ). This broader inclusion may account for some variability in outcomes, but it underscores the importance of vaccination across different cancer types. In terms of vaccine safety, our observations regarding adverse events are consistent with those reported by Javadinia 2022 , who noted that COVID‐19 vaccination in adults with cancer is generally well‐tolerated regardless of cancer type. Both systemic and local adverse events, including fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, asthenia, vomiting, headaches, muscle and joint pain, chills, transient lymphadenopathy, and injection site reactions, were reported across various studies. While Javadinia 2022 highlighted that most vaccine‐related side effects were grade two at most, they also pointed out the challenges posed by differing assessment methods across studies, which complicate meta‐analysis efforts, such as the lack of reporting on the exact prevalence of PCR‐confirmed COVID‐19 infections and their outcomes. Additionally, many studies included in their review lacked a control group or used healthy controls, complicating the analysis still further ( Javadinia 2022 ). Our review reveals notable gaps in the literature concerning other vaccines. Kamboj 2024 reported an absence of eligible studies for hepatitis B, tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccines. This lack of data aligns with our findings regarding the limited research available on certain vaccinations for adults with solid tumours. Furthermore, Kamboj 2024 identified only one RCT that examined the timing of pneumococcal vaccination. Authors' conclusions Implications for practice In adults with solid tumours, herpes zoster vaccines reduce the incidence of herpes zoster (high‐certainty evidence), although localised events at the injection site occur more frequently than with placebo or no vaccine (high‐certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether influenza vaccines affect all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, or serious adverse events (very‐low certainty evidence); the incidence of influenza was not measured in the studies. Vaccines for preventing COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in adults without prior infection (moderate‐certainty evidence), but they probably increase adverse events of any grade (moderate‐certainty evidence). We found no randomised controlled trials or controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions that investigated the use of vaccines compared to placebo or no vaccine for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, in adults with solid tumours. Implications for research We have identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines ( NCT05774171 ). Additional research, preferably RCTs, is necessary to assess a wider range of available vaccines against infectious diseases such as pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, for which we did not identify any RCTs or prospective NRSIs. This lack of research limits our understanding of how these vaccines perform in adults with solid tumours. While we advocate conducting RCTs to obtain robust evidence, if such studies are not possible for ethical reasons, retrospective (matched) analyses of individuals with cancer who have or have not received the respective vaccination could provide some insights. Future studies should include individuals of various age groups and those with different types of solid tumours undergoing diverse treatments (such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy). This diversity is crucial, because different age groups may respond differently to vaccines due to variations in immune system function, and individuals with solid tumours may be undergoing treatments that affect their immune response. When investigating multiple malignancies, it is important to report results as subgroups. This approach allows researchers to identify specific populations that benefit most from vaccination and understand under which cancer therapies the vaccines may be less effective in preventing infection. Additionally, it needs to be investigated whether passive immunisation with monoclonal antibodies may offer more protection than vaccines for immunocompromised or immunosuppressed individuals. Research should not just focus on the usual immunological laboratory parameters, especially in populations where established correlates of protection are still lacking. The outcomes measured should be patient‐centred and important, such as the incidence of infection (tracking how often vaccinated individuals contract the targeted infectious disease), quality of life (assessing how vaccination impacts patients' overall well‐being and daily functioning), all‐cause mortality (evaluating whether vaccination correlates with mortality rates amongst individuals with solid tumours), and adverse events (monitoring any negative side effects resulting from vaccination). Additionally, studies should take into account periods when the risk of infection is heightened. For instance, during flu season (typically October to March), individuals with compromised immune systems may face increased risks. Future research should investigate potential effect modifiers that could influence the effectiveness of vaccines for preventing infectious diseases. These might include patient demographics (age, sex, comorbidities) and treatment modalities (type and timing of cancer therapies). Importantly, future research must also address the unique challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), where barriers such as limited healthcare infrastructure, vaccine availability, and socioeconomic factors can significantly impact vaccination efforts. By understanding how these characteristics impact vaccine efficacy in LMIC contexts, alongside other factors influencing outcomes in high‐income settings, healthcare providers can tailor vaccination strategies to individual patient needs more effectively. In summary, addressing these gaps through rigorous research will enhance our understanding of vaccine effects across diverse patient populations. By prioritising patient‐centred outcomes and considering various factors influencing vaccine efficacy, including those specific to LMICs, we can optimise vaccination strategies to improve health outcomes for individuals at risk for infectious diseases. between protocol and review Differences between the published protocol ( Bora 2023 ) and this full review are as follows. Title We made minor edits to the title in order to use UK spelling ('tumours') and Cochrane style, i.e. 'for preventing' rather than 'for the prevention of'. Objectives We changed the wording from "To assess the benefits and harms of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours" to "To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours." Type of interventions We changed the wording to "We included vaccines for the prevention of the following infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours" and listed the diseases of the vaccines they protect against instead of the pathogens to specify the diseases targeted by these vaccines. Types of outcome measures Instead of including studies regardless of the reported outcome data, we decided to categorise eligible studies that did not report any of the relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification'. We previously listed 'local events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' under the outcome 'adverse events of special interest'. As these were intended to represent two separate outcomes, we no longer summarise them under one bullet point in the review but list them separately. Selection of studies We used the Rayyan software ( Ouzzani 2016 ) instead of Covidence to screen the references. We listed excluded studies that initially appeared to meet the inclusion criteria, but that we later excluded, in the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table, with the reasons for their exclusion, instead of listing all excluded studies. Search methods Although at least one RCT was identified for vaccines against influenza and COVID‐19, we searched for NRSIs, as the one RCT on influenza vaccines was published as correspondence only, and the one RCT on COVID‐19 reported on participants with solid tumours in a post hoc subgroup analysis. To ensure the integrity and reliability of the studies included in this review, we searched for errata or retractions related to the included studies that may have been published on MEDLINE, Embase, or Retraction Watch. We did not contact experts in the field to retrieve information on unpublished studies. If required, we contacted the authors for supplementary information. Assessment of reporting bias As we did not pool the data in the meta‐analysis and included fewer than 10 studies per comparison, we did not generate funnel plots to assess reporting bias. Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity We removed the planned subgroup analysis based on duration of follow‐up (e.g. shorter versus longer follow‐up) because we grouped the measurement time points of eligible outcomes into short‐term (up to 12 weeks after full vaccination), medium‐term (from 12 weeks to 6 months after full vaccination) and long‐term (more than 6 months after full vaccination) observations, if sufficient data was available (see Types of outcome measures ). Due to the limited number of studies that provided relevant data for our critical outcome, we did not perform meta‐analysis and thus conducted no subgroup analysis. If heterogeneity was above 75%, we planned to explore this with subgroup and sensitivity analysis. Despite considerable heterogeneity in Analysis 1.5 , we decided to keep the pooled effect estimate, as the effects of the individual studies were clearly on one side. We were unable to conduct the planned sensitivity analyses because the risk of bias for these RCTs was classified as either 'low' or 'some concerns'. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We created the summary of findings tables manually and did not use GRADEpro GDT . We added a section on consumer involvement during protocol development. The order of the comparisons and summary of findings tables was prioritised by clinical experts, based on relevance to decision‐makers. If evidence from both RCTs and NRSIs was available for a single outcome, only the RCT data were presented in the summary of findings tables. documents.title: Vaccines for preventing infections in adults with haematological malignancies.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vaccination aims to prevent infections. People who are immunocompromised, such as those with haematological malignancies, often experience higher immunosuppression, increasing their vulnerability to infections compared to individuals with solid tumours or healthy individuals.
OBJECTIVES: The aim of this review is to summarise and evaluate the benefits and risks of vaccines for preventing infections in adults with haematological malignancies.
SEARCH METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive systematic search in CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and Web of Science on 2 December 2024 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs). We also searched ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO (World Health Organization) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included RCTs and controlled NRSIs evaluating the preventive effect of vaccines on outcomes prioritised by clinical experts, patients, and patient representatives. The prioritised outcomes for adults (≥ 18 years) with haematological malignancies (excluding those receiving cellular therapies) were infection incidence, all-cause mortality, quality of life, adverse events of any grade, serious adverse events, and adverse events of special interest. We looked for studies that evaluated a broad range of vaccine types (e.g. COVID-19, diphtheria, Haemophilus influenzae type b, hepatitis B, herpes zoster, influenza, Neisseria meningitidis, pertussis, polio, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or tetanus), but we excluded live-attenuated vaccines.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We followed current Cochrane methodological standards in the conduct of this review. We assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane risk of bias 2 tool (RoB 2) for RCTs and Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) for controlled NRSIs.
MAIN RESULTS: We included six studies (four RCTs, two controlled NRSIs) with a total of 25,886 participants. We present the RCT results here and the NRSI findings from NRSIs in the full review. We judged one RCT on herpes zoster to be at low risk of bias overall, and we had 'some concerns' about bias in the other RCT on herpes zoster. We had 'some concerns' about bias in the RCTs on COVID-19 and influenza vaccines. Herpes zoster vaccines Two RCTs, involving 3067 participants with a range of haematological malignancies, evaluated vaccines for preventing herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine. Vaccines may reduce herpes zoster incidence up to 21 months post-vaccination, although the 95% CI includes the possibility of no effect (4% versus 6%; RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.07 to 2.23; 2 RCTs, 3067 participants; low-certainty evidence). Vaccines probably have little to no effect on all-cause mortality up to 28 days post-vaccination (2.7% versus 2.6%; RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.64; 2548 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Vaccines slightly increase any-grade adverse events within 30 days (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.18; 3110 participants; high-certainty evidence), but probably do not increase serious adverse events within 12 months (23% versus 29%; RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.05; 562 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) after vaccination. Vaccines increase injection site adverse events substantially (40% versus 13%; RR 3.07, 95% CI 2.62 to 3.59; high-certainty evidence) and also increase systemic adverse events (10% versus 6%; RR 1.82, 95% CI 1.38 to 2.40; high-certainty evidence), as measured in 2548 participants within 28 days post-vaccination. Neither RCT reported quality of life. COVID-19 vaccines One RCT, involving 95 participants with lymphoma, leukaemia or myeloma, evaluated the BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine compared to placebo or no vaccine. Evidence about the effect of BNT162b2 vaccine on the incidence of COVID-19 up to six months after the second dose compared to placebo or no vaccine remains very uncertain (2.2% versus 2%; RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.07 to 17.25; 1 RCT, 95 participants; very low certainty evidence). Regarding safety data (mixed population including both solid tumours and haematological malignancies), BNT162b2 vaccine probably increases the number of participants with any grade adverse events (35% versus 17.5%; RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.30; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and there may be little to no difference concerning the number of participants experiencing serious adverse events (2.4% versus 1.7%; RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.54; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; low-certainty evidence). The RCT did not report all-cause mortality, quality of life, injection site adverse events or systemic adverse events. Influenza vaccines No RCTs evaluated an influenza vaccine versus placebo or no vaccine. One RCT, involving 122 participants with plasma cell disorders, evaluated different dosing regimens for an influenza vaccine on the incidence of influenza infection. Evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of two doses of high-dose trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine compared to one dose (with strength based on age) of influenza vaccination on the incidence of infection within the 2015 to 2016 flu season (4% versus 8%; RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.11 to 2.08; very low-certainty evidence). The RCT did not report all-cause mortality, quality of life, any-grade or serious adverse events, or injection site or systemic adverse events.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: The evidence on vaccines for preventing infections in adults with haematological malignancies is limited and uncertain. Herpes zoster vaccines may reduce infection risk for up to 21 months, but the certainty of the evidence is low. While there is a considerable increase in short-term adverse events (high-certainty evidence), no increase in serious adverse events was observed at up to 12 months (moderate-certainty evidence). Data on long-term impacts on other outcomes are lacking. For COVID-19 and influenza vaccines, the evidence is very uncertain. We found no studies that could be included in the review of vaccines for our other infectious diseases of interest: diphtheria, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, Neisseria meningitidis, pertussis, polio, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or tetanus. Our review underscores the need for high-quality RCTs and controlled NRSIs with better reporting, larger samples, longer follow-ups, and a focus on patient-relevant outcomes, such as quality of life and long-term safety. A robust and continuously updated evidence base is essential to guide clinical and public health decisions.

documents.title: Respiratory diseases in survivors of adult cancer compared with the general population: a systematic review protocol.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: There is concern that survivors of adult cancers may be at increased risk of respiratory infections and of exacerbations of pre-existing respiratory conditions. Considering the high prevalence of respiratory disease in the general population, increased respiratory disease risk in survivors of adult cancers could translate into an important impact on morbidity and mortality. The aim of this systematic review is to summarise and assess the quality of all studies comparing respiratory outcomes between adult cancer survivors and individuals with no history of cancer.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This systematic literature review will be conducted using Medline, EMBASE and Cochrane. We will include cohort or case-control studies that provide a comparative estimate of the risk of a respiratory disease of interest in survivors of adult cancer against a comparator cohort of cancer-free individuals. No geographic, time or language restrictions will be applied. We will assess the risk of bias using the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network methodology checklists. Results will be summarised by type of respiratory outcome, cancer type and cancer survivorship definition. If sufficient numbers of homogeneous studies are found, summary measures of association will be calculated using random effects meta-analysis models.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval is not applicable to our study. The results will be used to identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research to understand respiratory morbidity in survivors of adult cancers and identify possible mitigation strategies. Results from this review will be disseminated to clinical audiences and submitted to a peer-reviewed journal when completed.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: This study has been registered on PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42022311557).

Strengths and limitations of this study The search terms for respiratory outcomes are comprehensive and clinically reviewed by a respiratory clinician. Risk of bias will be formally assessed in a structured and standardised way using the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network methodology checklists. No geographic, time or language restrictions will be applied in an attempt to find all eligible studies. The search will be conducted in English language within English databases; thus we may miss relevant articles not captured by English language search engines. Introduction Currently, 50% of people diagnosed with cancer are expected to survive for 10 or more years. 1 The proportion is likely to increase further considering the rapid and continual improvements in cancer management and treatment. As more patients survive longer, they may experience additional health challenges during their survivorship. There is evidence that cancer survivors are at an increased risk of developing certain adverse outcomes, such as cardiovascular diseases 2 and mental health issues, 3 that may cause morbidity and impaired quality of life. However, the long-term respiratory consequences of cancer and its treatment are less clear. Respiratory diseases have an immense worldwide burden of morbidity and mortality, accounting for more than 10% of all disability-adjusted life-years, second only to cardiovascular diseases (including stroke). 4 Furthermore, cancer can weaken the immune system which may increase the risk of respiratory infections. 5 Additionally, survivors of cancer often have a higher health burden. A quarter of patients with cancer have pre-existing respiratory comorbidities 6 and there is concern that cancer and its treatment or shared risk factors may be conducive to worse outcomes than in the general population. 7 Considering the high prevalence of respiratory disease in the general population, even a small increase in respiratory disease risk in cancer survivors will translate into an important impact on morbidity and mortality. Thus, identifying possible strategies to mitigate respiratory morbidity in cancer survivors would suppose an important improvement in absolute terms. We aim to conduct a systematic review to summarise and assess the quality of the current knowledge from studies comparing survivors of adult cancer to individuals with no history of cancer for respiratory outcomes. We aim to evaluate relative risks of a broad spectrum of respiratory outcomes across a wide range of cancer types, in order to build a complete picture of the evidence on respiratory health during cancer survivorship. Methods and analysis This study protocol has been designed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P), registered in the International Prospective Register of Ongoing Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) and will be reported according to the PRISMA reporting guidelines. PROSPERO registration number: CRD42022311557. Objectives The specific objectives of this study are: Summarise the current evidence on the association between cancer survivorship and incident respiratory disease outcomes. We will consider the relative risk of incident diagnosis, exacerbations (considered as primary care visits or hospitalisations) and mortality outcomes separately for each respiratory disease of interest between survivors of adult cancer and the cancer-free population. Critically appraise the quality of the available evidence and evaluate the main sources of bias. Identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research on respiratory health in cancer survivors. Search strategy The search will include articles published in Cochrane, Medline and EMBASE through to 8 March 2022. No geographic, time or language restrictions will be applied. We will use OVID search interface to simultaneously search both Medline and EMBASE and we will conduct a separate search within Cochrane. The coverage of EMBASE spans from 1974, Medline from 1946 and Cochrane Reviews from 1996. We do not plan to include grey literature as epidemiological studies providing measures of effect with enough information to be assessable are likely to be published in academic journals. Furthermore, we do not plan to routinely contact all study authors. We will search title, abstract and subject headings using our created search expression. The search expression will include keywords and subject headings (both Medical Subject Headings and Emtree) for the target population (survivors of adult cancer) and the target outcomes (respiratory diseases). As an additional step to identify studies that may have been missed by the initial search strategy, we will examine the reference lists of all studies identified in the initial database search that meet the selection criteria. We defined respiratory disease as any upper or lower respiratory condition. See table 1 for list of included respiratory diseases. Table 1 Categorisation of respiratory diseases included in the systematic literature review Category Conditions of interest COVID-19 Infection with SARS-CoV-19 Upper respiratory infections Nasopharyngitis, rhinitis, pharyngitis, sinusitis, tonsilitis, laryngitis, tracheitis, laryngotracheitis Bronchitis Acute bronchitis Influenza Influenza Pneumonia Pneumonia Asthma Asthma COPD Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis, emphysema Pneumonitis Pneumonitis Fibrosis Pulmonary fibrosis Interstitial lung disease Interstitial lung disease Screening The screening will be conducted in two stages: Screening of titles and abstracts: titles and abstracts will be screened against the selection criteria by one reviewer. A second reviewer will screen a random sample of 10% of articles identified in the initial search. Any discrepancies will be resolved by discussion between the reviewers and the wider study team. Studies which meet all the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria (see below) will be considered for full-text review. If the study cannot be unequivocally excluded during this phase, it will be considered for full-text review. Full-text review: this step will be conducted independently by two reviewers in full. Any discrepancies will be resolved by discussion between the reviewers and the wider study team. We will use the reference manager Endnote V.20 to store citations and screen all identified references. Selection criteria The inclusion criteria for the systematic review will be: The exposure is cancer survivorship. In this review, our focus will be on the survivorship period after initial active cancer treatment, so the exposed group must include follow-up time beyond the period of active treatment or the first year since diagnosis. The focus is on survivors of adult cancer; thus we will only include studies where individuals were aged≥18 years at diagnosis. The study evaluates at least one respiratory disease of interest as an outcome of interest (see table 1 for details). The study involves a comparator cohort of cancer-free individuals or a general population estimate used to calculate indirect measures such as standardised mortality Ratios. No other criteria will be set for the comparator. The study has an observational longitudinal cohort, matched cohort or case–control design. The study provides a relative measure of effect for a respiratory disease of interest in individuals with cancer compared with cancer-free controls. Examples of relevant measures of effect are relative risk ratios, ORs, rate ratios and hazard ratios. If studies provide sufficient information on measures of frequency for any of the respiratory diseases of interest measured in individuals with cancer and cancer-free controls to allow the calculation measure of effect between the groups, the study will also be included. We will exclude: Duplicate studies, defined as repeated articles, using the remove duplicate function of the software prior to conducting the manual screening. Any articles not identified by the software, will be removed manually by the reviewers. Studies where the exposed group is exclusively composed of patients with cancer under active treatment as well as cancer cohorts whose average follow-up time is≤1 year. Studies in which the exposed group includes individuals without cancer (eg, families and caregivers of the patient). Intervention studies, cross-sectional studies and studies that do not use original data (such as review articles, comments, letters, editorials and protocols). Any review study will be excluded but flagged and the citation lists will be evaluated in order to identify potentially eligible studies that were not captured in our search. Conference abstracts will be excluded if no corresponding full-text journal article is found as we consider that the information in an abstract will not be sufficient to complete our data extraction nor conduct an accurate bias assessment. While articles will not be excluded on the basis of language, practical limitations mean that we will only evaluate those studies captured by an English search strategy. Articles in languages not spoken by the study team will be translated using translation software. We will exclude full-text articles which are written in non-roman alphabets due to the limitations of our translation software. Reasons for exclusion will be collected in a cascade manner, meaning that papers that fail to meet any of the selection criteria will be automatically excluded and not further assessed. Where multiple papers are found to report data conducted on the same study population sample, these will be flagged, but not excluded. The results of these studies cannot be considered independent and thus the inclusion and/or interpretation of these studies will be considered on a case-by-case basis after discussion within the study team. Any inclusion or exclusion of studies of this type will be detailed in the data extraction phase and reported in the Results section of the report. Data extraction Data will initially be extracted from included studies into a spreadsheet. Data extraction will commence in July 2022. At minimum, we will detail information on the study article, population sample description, study design, exposure, comparator and outcome definitions, follow-up, measures of effect, measures of frequency and statistical methodology. The exact data items extracted are listed in box 2 . Box 2 Data items for extraction Data items: Administrative: Authors Journal Year of publication Financial/funding sources Conflict of interest reported Data/design/population: Country/countries of origin Data source Time period covered Study setting Study design Sample size Comparison group: Selection criteria of the comparison group Mean age of the comparison group Exposure: Selection criteria for exposed group Definition of cancer survivorship Time since cancer diagnosis (summary stats) Cancer stage (summary stats) Outcome: Respiratory disease category Respiratory disease definition Duration of follow-up (if applicable) Statistical methods: Statistical method for the calculation of estimates Statistical method for the calculation of the method of precision List of confounders included in the adjusted analysis (if applicable) Results Measure of frequency + precision estimate (comparison group) Measure of frequency + precision estimate (exposed group) Measure of effect + precision estimate (crude) Measure of effect +precision estimate (adjusted) When multiple different respiratory disease conditions or cancer types are reported in the same study, we will record or calculate information for all cancer types and respiratory outcomes. When multiple estimates are reported for the same condition (eg, if probable and confirmed influenza were reported as separate outcomes), we will only record or calculate the measure of effect for the outcome corresponding to the stronger certainty of diagnosis (in our illustrative example, we would select confirmed influenza). For each outcome we will record both the crude and adjusted effect measures as well as the list of confounders included in the adjusted analysis. If the results are stratified by severity, we will record all severity categories for said outcome. Risk of bias assessment We will use the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) methodology checklists as guidance to assess the risk of bias for each study design. The checklists are provided in online supplemental appendix 1 . In brief, we will assess if the study has a focussed aim, and whether there were opportunities for bias in the definition of the exposures and outcomes, selection of the study population and comparator group, and potential differential losses during follow-up. We will also assess how each study addresses confounding. Supplementary data bmjopen-2022-066029supp001.pdf Data analysis We will initially present the key characteristics and results of all studies in descriptive tables. We will stratify the presentation of results by likely sources of heterogeneity such as cancer type and respiratory disease category (see table 1 ). If sufficient studies are found, we will also stratify by different population definitions (ie, if we find multiple definitions for cancer survivorship). We will meta-analyse groups of studies if we find sufficient studies that are sufficiently homogeneous in terms of population and outcomes for which the calculation of a summary measure would be meaningful. In the case that a summary estimate is calculated, we will use random-effects model. We will explore the consistency between studies by using the I 2 statistic. Patient and public involvement No patients were involved in the development of this protocol Ethics and dissemination To our knowledge, no comparable review has previously been conducted on respiratory outcomes in survivors of adult cancer. We aim to identify all available literature on a wide range of respiratory outcomes and cancer types considered, with no language, geographical or date limitations. This will provide a comprehensive picture of the spectrum of respiratory conditions that affect cancer survivors as well as understand if cancer-specific or respiratory condition-specific associations have been noted in the literature. Considering the high prevalence of respiratory disease in the general population, even a small increase in respiratory disease risk in cancer survivors will translate into an important impact on morbidity and mortality. The results of this review can be used to better understand respiratory morbidity in cancer survivors, identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research, and help devise possible mitigation strategies. Results will be disseminated to clinical audiences and may support clinicians and decision-makers in developing survivorship care guidelines. While this protocol has been developed according to the PRISMA-P guidelines and has been registered on PROSPERO (ref: PROSPERO CRD42022311557), some potential limitations are worth noting. First, there is currently no universally accepted definition of cancer survivorship, 8 and this review focusses on the late respiratory challenges of cancer and its treatment. Consequentially, we have adopted the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer definition which defines cancer survivor as ‘individuals diagnosed with cancer who have completed their primary treatment (maintenance treatment can be ongoing)’. 9 We have used an inclusive approach towards this definition and will consider that the period of active treatment is expected to have been completed after 1 year since diagnosis, thus we will not exclude studies that include patients from cancer diagnosis with a mean follow-up of <1 year. 10 Studies comparing long-term outcomes in cancer survivors and controls may be subject to a number of biases including selection bias, detection bias and competing-risks. We will evaluate the risk of bias in each included study in order to aid the interpretation of results, though we acknowledge that not all types of bias are specifically addressed by the SIGN checklists. Our review will also have other limitations. We may miss some relevant studies due to an imperfect search strategy, though hand searching of reference lists should identify additional papers and allow us to refine our search terms if needed. Finally, we are not including conference abstracts or preprints which could potentially exclude some relevant results. Considering the high prevalence of respiratory disease in the general population, even a small increase in respiratory disease risk in cancer survivors will translate into an important impact on morbidity and mortality. The results of this review can be used to better understand respiratory morbidity in cancer survivors, identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research, and help devise possible mitigation strategies.
